newsitem.title: USA: Saudi bombing suspect to be brought to U.S.
newsitem.headline: Saudi bombing suspect to be brought to U.S.

text.p: A Saudi man implicated in the 1996 truck bombing that killed 19 members of the U.S. Air Force in Saudi Arabia is expected to be sent from Canada to the United States on Tuesday, U.S. officials said.

They said the suspect, Hani Abdel-Rahim Hussein al-Sayegh, was expected to appear in U.S. District Court here on Wednesday and plead guilty to conspiracy charges involving an unrelated attack plotted in the Middle East, but never carried out.
Sayegh has been identified in Canadian court documents as the driver of a car that gave the go-ahead signal for the bomb-laden truck involved in the attack on Khobar Towers.
FBI officials have long sought to question Sayegh about the June attack on the compound that housed U.S. military personnel in Dhahran in eastern Saudi Arabia.
As part of the tentative plea deal that has been reached, Sayegh would cooperate with U.S. authorities and tell them what he knows about the Khobar Towers bombing last June, the officials said.
"Everything is all set," one official said of the deportation and court appearance.

Two U.S. Justice Department officials initially said Sayegh's deportation would not occur on Tuesday, but other officials later said his move had to be pushed forward because of extensive publicity about his case in the news media.
Although the officials cautioned that the plans still could change again, they said Sayegh was due in the United States sometime on Tuesday.

In New York, Sayegh's lawyer, Michael Wildes, told Reuters a deal has been reached on the deportation. "I expect him on U.S. soil shortly. A deal has been cut," the former federal prosecutor said in a telephone interview.

Wildes said he would appear with Sayegh in federal court here in the next few days. He added, "They will be able to investigate the Khobar Towers bombing and get some pretty serious intelligence information in that regard."
U.S. officials for months have been seeking independent verification of allegations by Saudi Arabia that Iran was responsible for the attack. Iran has denied any involvement.
The conspiracy charge involving Sayegh concerned an aborted attack against the United States that was plotted about six months before the Khobar Towers bombing, the officials said.
Sayegh was arrested last March under a Canadian warrant alleging that he was a "security risk to Canada;" he has been held in a prison in Ottawa since then
